source: Wheeler (2013) Is cognition embedded or extended? The case of gestures
finding: Wheeler separates three claims. Conservative embedded: gestures only help neural thinking. Radical embedded: gestures are part of thinking but only inside the skin. Extended: gestures and outside things are part of thinking. He concludes that gesture arguments alone support only the conservative embedded view.
numbers: Three-way split. No new experiment; a philosophy chapter.
quote: gestures help us to think, but (in the relevant sense) they are not themselves part of thinking
limits: A philosophical argument, not data. Wheeler is himself a fan of extended cognition and calls the result disappointing.
agent_relevance: Safe reading for a scaffold: an external aid improves reasoning without needing to be counted as part of the mind. No design change needed.

source: Goldin-Meadow, Nusbaum, Kelly, Wagner (2001) Explaining math: gesturing lightens the load, as reported in Wheeler (2013)
finding: Children memorised a list, then solved a maths problem, then recalled the list. Those allowed to gesture during the maths recalled more of the list. Reading: gesture takes load off neural resources.
numbers: Matched child groups, gesture free versus told not to gesture. Wheeler gives no effect size.
limits: Secondary report only. The original PDF could not be fetched this session. Wheeler warns that offloading to a prop does not make the prop cognitive (his phone-number example).
agent_relevance: Dual-task logic is a clean test pattern: measure what a tool frees up, not only the main score.

source: Broaders, Cook, Mitchell, Goldin-Meadow (2007) and Hutchins (2010), as reported in Wheeler (2013)
finding: Children asked to gesture while explaining new maths problems showed correct strategies in gesture that were absent from speech, and then learned more from a later lesson than children told not to gesture. Hutchins describes a flight instructor whose gesture indexes an imagined event that is a precondition for what the speech refers to.
numbers: No numbers given in Wheeler. Gesture-speech mismatch is used as a sign of readiness to learn.
limits: Secondary report. Wheeler offers two readings: gesture is a window on a covert neural strategy, or gesture itself creates new content.
agent_relevance: Implicit knowledge can show in one channel before another. Compare an agent's draft, plan and final answer for mismatch.

source: Clark (2008) cognitive self-stimulation, as analysed in Wheeler (2013)
finding: Clark says gestures are self-generated inputs that loop back to neural processing and turbo-charge thought, like exhaust driving a turbocharger. He names three loop kinds: fully anarchic, semi-anarchic, centrally controlled, and rules out fully anarchic for gesture. Wheeler agrees that an input can still count as cognitive but says Clark's argument does not show gestures are constitutive.
numbers: Three loop types. Wheeler also tests Gallagher's prenoetic argument and finds it insufficient.
quote: gestures are self-generated inputs to neural processing that (to borrow one of Clark's own analogies) turbo-charge thought
limits: Theory only, no measurement. Wheeler paraphrases Clark.
agent_relevance: A self-stimulation loop maps to an agent writing a note and reading it back. The loop is the mechanism, not the medium.

source: Pouw, de Nooijer, van Gog, Zwaan, Paas (2014) Toward a more embedded/extended perspective on the cognitive function of gestures
finding: Review in Frontiers in Psychology. Claims current theories are disembodied because they treat gestures as outputs of internal sensorimotor states. Proposes gestures are external tools of the cognitive system that give a stable physical and visual presence to think with. Main principle: when internal computation is costly, people adopt an external strategy, environment or gesture, if it is cheap.
numbers: Principle quoted from Kirsh 2010 in the paper: cognitive processes flow to wherever it is cheaper to perform them. Gives testable predictions: slow a mouse rotation tool, add wrist weights, and see when gesture use changes.
quote: gestures are external physical tools of the cognitive system that replace and support otherwise solely internal cognitive processes
limits: Position paper. The authors state they take no side on extended versus embedded. Predictions were only partly tested later (see the 2020 Tower of Hanoi study).
agent_relevance: The cost-trade-off rule is usable: an agent should call a tool or write notes when internal reasoning cost is high, not by default.

source: Goldin-Meadow et al. (2001) as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Participants who remembered letters while explaining a hard maths problem remembered more letters when allowed to gesture than when not allowed. Taken to show gesture cuts working-memory load.
numbers: No counts given in Pouw 2014. Hostetter and Alibali 2008 add that the effect held both when the experimenter imposed gesture inhibition and when participants inhibited on their own.
limits: Secondary report. Exact means and test statistics not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for offloading: gesture frees capacity for a second task.

source: Chu and Kita (2008, 2011), as reported in Pouw et al. (2014) plus an abstract snippet
finding: In mental rotation, people first gesture as if holding the object, later use a flat hand as stand-in, and gesture less over time. Encouraging gesture raised mental rotation performance. Lower spatial working memory predicted more gestures. A search snippet of the 2011 abstract says gesture-encouraged participants beat gesture-allowed and gesture-prohibited ones in Experiment 2, and the benefit carried into a later no-gesture block and a paper folding task in Experiment 3.
numbers: No group means retrieved.
limits: Secondary report plus snippet. The full Chu and Kita PDF returned 403 in this session, so means and test statistics are missing.
agent_relevance: Gesture use shrinks with skill, a sign of internalisation. Scaffolds may help most on novel tasks and be droppable later.

source: Alibali, Spencer, Knox, Kita (2011) gear problem, as reported in Pouw (2014) and Marghetis and Bergen (2014)
finding: With gesture allowed, people more often simulated each gear with the fingers (depictive strategy). With gesture prohibited, they more often used the parity rule. The depictive group was not more accurate. Preschoolers who gestured more later found the parity rule more efficiently (Boncoddo 2010).
numbers: No counts in either review. Marghetis and Bergen say gesturing made the sensorimotor strategy more likely than both spontaneous no-gesture trials and inhibited trials.
limits: Secondary report. Shows gesture changes which strategy is chosen, not necessarily accuracy.
agent_relevance: A tool can steer strategy without raising accuracy. Measure strategy mix as well as score.

source: Kirsh and Maglio 1994, Ballard 1995, Gray and Fu 2004, Kirsh 2009, Risko 2013, Martin and Schwartz 2005, as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Parallel embedded-cognition evidence. Expert Tetris players rotate pieces physically (epistemic actions). People look back at a model just in time instead of memorising. In a VCR task people relied on memory when lookup cost a mouse click and on the screen when it cost a glance. People tilted their heads more with more letters and larger tilt. An external tic-tac-toe grid helped only in 4x4 and mostly for low spatial ability. Children aged 9 to 10 did better on fraction problems with movable tiles than with drawings.
numbers: Effect sizes not given in the review.
limits: Secondary report. Not gesture studies; Pouw uses them by analogy.
agent_relevance: Supports a cost-sensitive rule for external aids: use them when internal cost is high and external access is cheap.

source: Chu et al. (2013), Marstaller and Burianova (2013), Delgado et al. (2011), Kirsh (1995), as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Lower spatial working memory, spatial transformation and conceptualisation scores predicted more spontaneous representational gestures. People with low working memory were hurt more by not being allowed to gesture. Toddlers pointed more under memory demand. Allowed to point, people counted coins faster and with fewer errors.
numbers: No numbers in the review text.
limits: Secondary report. A later direct check found working-memory capacity did not predict who gestured (Pouw 2020).
agent_relevance: Benefit seems concentrated in low-capacity users. Weaker models may gain more from scaffolds than strong ones.

source: Rival theories GSA, LGP, IPH and IMT, as compared in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Four accounts compared. Gesture-as-simulated-action: gestures are by-products of motor simulation. Lexical gesture process (Krauss 2000): gesture feedback primes word retrieval. Information packaging (Kita 2000): gesture chunks images for speech. Image maintenance (Wesp 2001): gesture refreshes visuospatial images in working memory. Pouw judges only image maintenance as clearly giving gestures-as-acts a job.
numbers: Wesp et al. 2001, via Hostetter and Alibali 2008: more than twice as many gestures describing a painting from memory as with it present.
quote: gestures keep the non-lexical concept in memory during the lexical search
limits: The ranking is Pouw's own view. He says the other theories are not wrong, only silent on this question.
agent_relevance: Different mechanisms predict different effects: memory refresh, retrieval cue, chunking. Match a scaffold to the mechanism that applies.

source: Hostetter and Alibali (2008) Visible embodiment: Gestures as simulated action
finding: Founding model of GSA. Perceptual and motor simulations in imagery and speech activate premotor states. Activation spreads to motor areas and a gesture appears when strength passes a gesture threshold. Three factors: simulation strength, threshold height, and the motor system already engaged by speech. Gesture rides along with the speech motor plan, like activation through a gate.
numbers: Threshold depends on neural coupling, cognitive effort (inhibiting gesture costs resources) and social setting. Cites Hostetter, Alibali, Kita 2007: more gestures for dot patterns that must be parsed into shapes.
quote: When this spreading activation occurs, a gesture is born.
limits: Conceptual model with no quantitative fit. It makes gesture the default and not gesturing the costly act, so gestures get no active job. Pouw 2014 attacks that point.
agent_relevance: Little direct design value. Useful as the null story: gestures may be a symptom of thinking, not a help.

source: Hostetter and Alibali (2008) on speech-production accounts and tip-of-the-tongue evidence
finding: Lexical access: gesture rates rise when words are hard to find, and blocking gesture lowers fluency. Frick-Horbury and Guttentag (1998) found that restricting gesture in tip-of-the-tongue states raised retrieval failures, but Beattie and Coughlan (1998) found conflicting results. Information packaging: gestures break images into chunks for speech.
numbers: No numbers for these studies in the review.
limits: Evidence on lexical retrieval is mixed. Pouw 2014 cites Hoetjes et al. (2014) as a case where banning gesture did not disrupt speech as expected.
agent_relevance: Mixed record on one of the oldest claims. Treat gesture benefits as task-specific, not general.

source: Marghetis and Bergen (2014) Embodied meaning, inside and out: the coupling of gesture and mental simulation
finding: Argues simulation and gesture are bidirectionally coupled in speaker and listener. Simulation drives gesture: describing patterns they had made themselves led to more gestures than patterns they had only viewed (Hostetter and Alibali 2010). Gesture shapes simulation: in Beilock and Goldin-Meadow (2010) switching Tower of Hanoi disk weights hurt only people who had explained their first solution, and the effect tracked how much their gestures showed weight.
numbers: Chapter gives no sample sizes. Goldin-Meadow et al. (2012) is cited: gesture helps mental rotation only if produced, not merely seen.
limits: Review chapter. Effect sizes not given.
agent_relevance: Producing a representation changes the representation. For an agent, writing out a step may add detail it did not hold before.

source: Aldugom, Fenn, Cook (2020) Gesture during math instruction specifically benefits learners with high visuospatial working memory capacity
finding: Adults watched a video lesson in a new maths system. With gesture in the lesson, visuospatial working memory predicted learning. Without gesture, verbal working memory predicted it. First adult study linking working-memory differences to learning with gesture.
numbers: Study 1: 64 analysed after excluding 11 of 75. Posttest mean 0.75 (SD 0.21), transfer 0.61 (SD 0.24). Transfer: visuospatial beta 0.43, z 2.17, p .030; verbal beta 0.011, p .95; ACT beta 0.47, p .017. Visuospatial-ACT r .61.
limits: Gesture is seen by learners here, not made by the thinker. Posttest visuospatial effect only marginal (beta 0.42, p .074). Correlational.
agent_relevance: The same scaffold recruits different capacities depending on its form. Check which skill a scaffold leans on.

source: Pouw, Mavilidi, van Gog, Paas (2020) Co-thought gesturing supports more complex problem solving in subjects with lower visual working memory
finding: Tower of Hanoi, silent solving. Gesturing, spontaneous or instructed, gave faster solutions on the hard 4-disc task, but only for people with low visual working memory. No such interaction for spatial working memory (Corsi blocks).
numbers: 76 recruited, 73 analysed. On 4-disc: non-gesturing n=19, solution time 103.0 s (SD 65.3); spontaneous n=18, 70.9 s (SD 54.4); instructed n=35, 80.1 s (SD 53.6). Steps about equal (24.2, 23.7, 22.8). Spontaneous gesturing 28.9% (11/38) on 3-disc and 47.3% (18/38) on 4-disc, McNemar chi2(1)=4.00, p=.039.
limits: Gain is in time, not steps. Spontaneous gesturers were not reliably the low-capacity people (VPT t(34) = -1.87, p .071), against the likelihood prediction. Small cells. 82.2% at ceiling on 3-disc steps.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the cost rule: effect shows with higher difficulty and lower capacity. Report scaffold gains by difficulty tier.

source: Pouw et al. (2020) manipulation check and design
finding: Instructed gesturers gestured about twice as often as spontaneous ones. Gesture rate rose with task complexity.
numbers: 3-disc mean gestures: spontaneous 23.45 (SD 13.87), instructed 47.70 (SD 25.78). 4-disc: 32.78 (SD 25.92) and 66.20 (SD 18.59). Complexity F(1,52)=26.62, p<.001, partial eta2 .339; group F(1,52)=43.05, p<.001, partial eta2 .453.
limits: Random assignment only between gesture-allowed and instructed. Spontaneous versus non-gesturing is self-selected, so the causal claim there is weak.
agent_relevance: Self-selected tool users differ from assigned users. Randomise tool use when testing a scaffold.

source: Hu, Ma et al. (2025) GesPrompt: Leveraging co-speech gestures to augment LLM-based interaction in virtual reality (DIS 2025)
finding: VR system where a GPT agent turns speech plus raw hand gesture into spatial commands. Study of 12 people. GesPrompt beat gesture-only and voice-only on time and usability, and users reported less mental effort than with voice-only.
numbers: N=12. Mean interaction time 43.65 s (SD 15.55) vs 91.11 s gesture-only and 108.58 s voice-only. SUS 86 vs 74 vs 59. Mental effort Likert (Q4): 4.00 (SD 0.23) vs 2.33 voice-only. Average total error 21.11%; rotation 28.33%, path 26.67%, position 23.33%.
limits: Gesture here is communication to the model, not the user's thinking aid. N=12, Likert scales, mostly male sample. Not a test of the gesture-as-tool theory.
agent_relevance: A model can read pointing and shape gestures for spatial detail. Evidence that gesture lowers prompting effort, not that it helps a model reason.

source: Hu, Ma et al. (2025) GesPrompt gesture parsing accuracy
finding: Parsing accuracy varied by shape. A straight line was parsed better than a circle or sine wave. Two hands gave smaller rotation error than one, not significantly.
numbers: Path similarity: line 95.25% (SD 2.34), circle 90.67% (SD 3.45, p .0031), sine 88.50% (SD 7.37, p .004). Rotation error 10.82 deg two hands vs 17.89 one hand. Object selection precision 100%, recall 96.56%.
limits: Small sample, one prototype. Accuracy depends on hand tracking, not only on language-model reasoning.
agent_relevance: Spatial intent through gesture is lossy for complex shapes; expect errors to grow with spatial complexity.

source: Large language models for virtual human gesture selection (2025)
finding: GPT-4 was prompted to choose co-speech gestures for utterances. Prompts that gave a fixed set of gestural intents produced more appropriate gestures and better alignment with the real speaker than open prompting. Two experts rated appropriateness.
numbers: Inference time 6.51 to 9.29 s per utterance with full output. When asked only for gesture type and phrase: 1.20 s GPT-4, 1.08 s GPT-4o-mini, 1.23 s Llama 3.1. Appropriateness percentages not extracted.
limits: About animating avatars, nothing to do with LLM thinking. Two expert raters who resolved disagreements by discussion.
agent_relevance: Constraining the output vocabulary improved quality, a general lesson for scaffold design.

source: Understanding co-speech gestures in-the-wild (JEGAL) (2025)
finding: Proposes three tasks (gesture retrieval, gesture word spotting, active speaker detection) and a tri-modal video-gesture-speech-text model that the authors say beats large vision-language models. Text-based spotting beat audio-based.
numbers: AVS-Spot test set 500 samples (100 stressed words, 400 not). Exact table values not reliably read because of two-column text extraction.
limits: A representation-learning paper, not about gesture aiding thought. Table reading uncertain.
agent_relevance: Gesture-word meaning can be learned from video; this is understanding, not use of gesture for reasoning.

source: Can vision language models understand mimed actions? (MIME) (2025)
finding: Benchmark of 86 mimed actions rendered from motion capture with character, background and viewpoint changes. Humans score near 100%. Vision-language models do far worse.
numbers: VLMs at most 52.3% in multiple choice and 19.8% in free form. Under adversarial perturbation all below 10%. Chain of thought did not consistently help; few-shot helped only API models. In 80% of Gemini 1.5 Flash chain-of-thought failures the gesture was described wrongly; 15% misread a correct description.
limits: Tests understanding of others' gestures, not thinking with gestures. Models tested date from early 2025 or older (Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4o mini, Qwen 2.5 VL).
agent_relevance: Perception of bodily movement is a weak point of vision models. Do not rely on a scaffold that depends on reading gestures.

source: Wheeler (2013) on the parity principle and the mark of the cognitive
finding: Wheeler lays out first-wave extended cognition (parity principle, Clark and Chalmers 1998) and second-wave (complementarity, integration). He prefers first-wave and argues second-wave stress on inner-outer differences makes extension harder to argue. Parity rests on functionalism and multiple realizability.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Philosophical. The quote is not reproduced here to avoid misquoting the trimmed text.
agent_relevance: Parity is the philosophical basis for treating a notebook or scratchpad as part of an agent's thought. Our scaffold needs the engineering, not the label.

source: Hatano and Osawa abacus work and Cook and Tanenhaus (2009), as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Intermediate abacus users gesture over an imagined abacus; advanced users rely less on gestures. In Tower of Hanoi explanation, people who used real disks gestured in line with the physical moves; those who used a computer simulation did not.
numbers: No numbers in the review text.
limits: Secondary report of older studies. Fading with skill supports internalisation.
agent_relevance: Support for scaffold fading: aids may help while a skill is acquired and drop away later.

source: Pouw et al. (2014) future-research list
finding: Proposes tests: vary the speed of a mouse-driven rotation tool to see if gesture use rises when the tool is slow; add weights at the wrists to raise gesture cost; track whether gesture shifts from as-if manipulation to stand-in as the task becomes familiar.
numbers: No data; predictions only.
limits: Untested in the paper. Pouw 2020 tests only the capacity prediction.
agent_relevance: Cost manipulations of a tool are a way to test when an agent should use it.

source: Delgado et al. (2011) pointing in children and Kirsh (1995) counting, as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: In two child studies (ages 2-4 and 4-6) solitary pointing rose under memory demand (hidden toy, 45-60 s delay) and constraining pointing hurt children who habitually pointed. Adults counting coins were faster and made fewer errors when allowed to point.
numbers: Task difficulty (540 degree table turn) had no effect on pointing in the first study. No other numbers given.
limits: Review-level report. The difficulty manipulation was null.
agent_relevance: A cheap external marker for position tracking is the simplest tool-like gesture; compare to an agent keeping a running tally.

source: Hostetter and Alibali (2008) on viewpoint and metaphoric gestures
finding: Character-viewpoint gestures come from simulated motor imagery; observer-viewpoint gestures from simulated visual imagery. Metaphoric gestures (palms balancing for fairness) come from simulated spatial image schemas. Gestures for ideas with no action simulation, like beautiful, should be rare.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Hostetter and Alibali 2007: speakers with stronger spatial skills gesture more.
limits: Conflicts with the compensation finding that low spatial ability predicts more gesture (Chu et al. 2013, via Pouw 2014). The sources do not reconcile the two.
agent_relevance: Abstract ideas can be given spatial structure. Spatial layout of ideas is a possible scaffold.

source: Schwartz and Black (1999) and Martin and Schwartz (2005), as reported in Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: People predicted whether water spills from tilted glasses much better when rotating empty glasses with eyes closed than when only imagining it. Children did better on fraction problems with movable tiles, and being shown the correct tile arrangement did not help.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Secondary report. About object manipulation, not gesture.
agent_relevance: Open-ended manipulation can find structure that a handed-over answer does not teach.

source: Pouw et al. (2014) own limits on the evidence
finding: Pouw concedes the evidence is not conclusive about when and how the cognitive system trades internal for external computation, and that the gear-problem depictive strategy was not more accurate than the parity rule.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: these findings do not allow us to draw definitive conclusions about when and how the cognitive system trades external with internal computational resources
limits: Quote taken from the paper text.
agent_relevance: Keep claims modest: strong evidence covers only a few lab tasks (rotation, Hanoi, gears, letter recall).
